idea: Frank Hurley's 1915 photograph of Shackleton's Endurance, rigging furred with frost and locked in the pack ice (white ink on black tee, halftone), captioned 'Crushed 1915. All 28 came home.' For people who prefer a story about leadership that ends well.

The 1873 Newfoundland photograph of a giant squid laid out on the shore (first known photograph of one), halftone, captioned 'First photographed 1873. Dead, and still unbelievable.' A nerdy nod to a creature science doubted for centuries.

The whaleship Charles W. Morgan at a New Bedford wharf, early 1900s archive photograph, captioned 'Launched 1841. Still afloat.' She is the last wooden whaleship in the world and sailed again in 2014.
The 1934 Beebe and Barton bathysphere, a steel ball hanging on a cable, halftone, captioned '923 metres down, on a cable.' For anyone who likes bravery with very little margin.
A museum photograph of a brass marine chronometer in its gimballed box, captioned 'Latitude was easy. Longitude needed a clock.' A small celebration of the problem that took a clockmaker to solve.

The wreck of the Peter Iredale on the Oregon beach, an archive photograph of the ribs in the sand, captioned 'Ran aground 1906. Still there.' It is dark humour about permanence, and the wreck can still be visited.

A Library of Congress photograph of a Mississippi sternwheeler with a deckhand sounding the river, captioned 'Mark twain. Two fathoms. Safe water.' That was the call that gave Samuel Clemens his pen name.
A close halftone of a lighthouse Fresnel lens from a Library of Congress survey photograph, captioned 'Someone has to stay up.' For night owls and anyone who keeps the lights on for others.
A Wilson Bentley snowflake photomicrograph (he photographed over 5,000 of them), white on black, captioned 'He checked. Over 5,000 times.' A weather shirt about patience and looking closely.
A archive photograph of a cumulonimbus anvil over open water, captioned 'Named by a pharmacist, 1802.' Luke Howard gave clouds their Latin names. It is a quiet, smart shirt for people who look up.

A hull photograph with the Plimsoll mark visible at the waterline, captioned 'Loaded to here. No further.' Samuel Plimsoll's load line became law in 1876, and the shirt is a polite boundary-setting joke.
A US Life-Saving Service surfmen breeches-buoy drill, archive halftone, captioned 'Rehearsed until boring. Then it mattered.' About training for the day nobody wants.
An archive portrait of lighthouse keeper Ida Lewis in her rowboat at Lime Rock, Rhode Island, captioned 'Rowed out. Again.' A tribute to a woman remembered for repeated rescues.
A tight halftone of a wandering albatross in flight (NOAA or museum archive), captioned 'Wingspan 3.5 metres. Barely flaps.' For people who admire effortless efficiency.
A Library of Congress harbour photograph at low tide, fishing boats tipped on the mud, captioned 'Twice a day, the harbour changes its mind.' For anyone who understands tides and moods alike.

A storm wave breaking over a lighthouse base, early 20th-century archive photograph, captioned 'Waves carry energy, not water.' The physics fact doubles as a point of view about what travels and what stays.
An archive photograph of a signalman holding two semaphore flags, captioned 'Message received.' A deadpan option for anyone who sends and receives with arms alone.
Fram, Nansen's polar ship, frozen into the Arctic ice, halftone, captioned 'Built to be squeezed.' Its rounded hull was designed so ice would lift it rather than crush it.
A historical photograph of a sailor splicing rope on a tall ship's deck, captioned 'A knot is a decision.' For makers and anyone who values something tied properly.
A Detroit Publishing Company photograph of a lone lighthouse on a rock in rough water, white on black, captioned 'Not lonely. On duty.' A pointed reframe for people who like their own company.
